children: Nvidia would like the market to focus on its European tour right now. But the chip maker is caught up in the artificial-intelligence debt fright as CEO Jensen Huang said the company doesn't need to intervene to help its partner CoreWeave.
Nvidia shares were down 1.9% at $217.15 Thursday. That was set to add to Wednesday's 3.2% loss as fears over AI spending gripped the market.

With a market valuation of more than $5 trillion and more cash than it knows what to do with, Nvidia is generally insulated from such panics. But this one hits a little closer to home as CoreWeave — the cloud-computing company with which Nvidia has close ties as both investor and supplier — is at the heart of the consternation due to rising yields on its debt.

"The fears are that if neo-clouds like CoreWeave have trouble securing financing, they will cancel orders for chips, memory, networking and token usage. That, in turn, will reduce the order backlog for companies such as Nvidia," wrote Tom Essaye, founder and president of Sevens Report.

That leaves the market watching to see if Nvidia will make an explicit statement of support for CoreWeave. But Huang said Thursday that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop as its cost of capital is decreasing, Bloomberg reported, citing comments at an event in Sweden.

As part of the companies' existing agreements, Nvidia is already obligated to purchase any unsold cloud-computing capacity through April 13, 2032, if CoreWeave's data centers aren't fully used by its own customers.

"This is not the first time we've had a sizable market wobble on the back of AI fears but as we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action," wrote Deutsche Bank analyst Jim Reid in a research note. "AI financing costs aren't dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges."

Meanwhile, Nvidia is still on a European charm offensive in the lead up to its GTC event in Berlin on Oct. 20-22. The latest initiative was the announcement this week of planned investments in five U.K. start-ups, specializing in sectors including biology and quantum computing. Such deals could be handy eventually by driving long-term demand for AI hardware.
But right now, the market is focused on CoreWeave and what it means for Nvidia.
